entry.title: I Don't Know How to Code. I'm Learning Anyway.
entry.summary: A_Zoology postgraduate's honest journey into the world of coding. **I have a BSc in Life Science and an MSc in Zoology. I know cells.i know organisms.i know how to sit with a research problem and think it through carefully. But code?not long ago, i couldn't even read a line of it-i didn't know what i was looking at, how it was meant to be read,or how it was meant to be written. So why did i start? Honestly-fear. i kept watching the world move faster,technology becoming the language of everything,and i felt something uncomfortable sitting in my chest. a quiet fear. what if i get left behind? not dramatically,not all at once-just slowly,quietly,becoming irrelevant in a world that was speaking a language i never learned. That fear was the first reason. The second was something harder to admit—I want to build my name in this field.i want a career here. I don't even fully know what that looks like yet. but the want is there.loud and clear,even when everything else is confusing. And the third reason-the one that actually gets me through the hard days-is curiosity.a real pull towards this whole world of coding.i don't fully understand it yet, but something about it draws me in. In the beginning,a missing comma or a stray hyphen made no sense to me. i didn't understand why they mattered,or how something so small could break everything.i'd stare at an error with no idea what i'd done wrong. Now, slowly,i've started noticing those small mistakes myself-usually after i run the code and it breaks.it's a tiny thing.but it's mine. So here i am.still at the beginning.learning on kaggle. making mistakes i'll probably write about here. This blog is not a tutorial. i have nothing to teach you yet. This is just a story told honestly, from inside the confusion. I hope you'll read along. _**

entry.title: Your Spring AI tests are slow, flaky, and cost money. Here's how to make them deterministic.
entry.summary: You wire up Spring AI, the ChatClient fluent API feels great, your feature works. Then you sit down to write a test — and every good option is bad. A test that calls a real model is: Slow. A hosted call is a second or two; run it on every branch and it adds up. Run inference locally (Ollama + Testcontainers) and a cold call is ~47 s. Either way it's not a loop you run on save. Expensive. Every run of every test is billable tokens — times every developer, times every CI job. Unrepeatable. The same prompt can answer differently tomorrow. A test that asserts on model output is flaky by construction. Untestable in CI.
